beats.text: May, eighteen thirty-three. A ship leaves Boston for India. Its cargo: one hundred eighty tons of ice.
Four months at sea. Straight across the equator.
The man behind it: Frederic Tudor. Years earlier, people had laughed at him. A Boston paper joked about a slippery speculation.
His ice was cut from frozen lakes in New England. Packed in sawdust. Stacked tight, so it would melt slowly.
But when the ship reached Calcutta, more than half was still frozen. A hundred tons.
So people in India drank ice-cold drinks, from American lakes. And Tudor became known as the Ice King.
Then came ice houses. Ice factories. And finally, the fridge.
Today, your freezer makes ice in a few hours, right in your kitchen.
One hundred eighty tons, four months at sea, for a cold drink. You just open the door.

sources: Ship Tuscany left Boston on 12 May 1833 with about 180 tons of ice packed in sawdust; arrived in Calcutta in early September 1833 with about 100 tons still frozen, after about four months. Frederic Tudor ('the Ice King'). American Heritage, 'Cold Mine'; Atlas Obscura, 'How did people get ice'; Scroll.in.

1806, Boston Gazette on Tudor's first ice cargo to Martinique: 'No joke. A vessel with a cargo of 80 tons of Ice has cleared out from this port for Martinique. We hope this will not prove to be a slippery speculation.' (quoted in Smithsonian Magazine / American Heritage). Film: 'S.S. Coptic Sailing Away' (Edison, 1897), public domain, illustrative (Internet Archive).
